sections.h2: How does an Iowa tax sale work?
sections.html:
Iowa counties sell delinquent property taxes at an annual public sale, and the buyer receives a certificate, not a deed. On the third Monday in June, the county treasurer offers all parcels with delinquent taxes for sale, although the treasurer may pick a different June date for good cause (Iowa Code 446.7).

The deed comes much later, and only if the owner and other interested parties do not redeem in time. That gap is what gives a homeowner room to act, and it is the reason a lien-style purchase is not the same as owning the house.

Parcels held by a county or city, or owned by the state or a political subdivision, cannot be sold, and a sale of them is void.

sections.h2: What leads up to the June sale?
sections.html:
Taxes first become late, then the owner gets notices, then the parcel is listed. The statewide treasurers' calendar shows the sequence.

WhenWhat happens
September 1First-half installment due, payable through September 30
OctoberUnpaid first half becomes delinquent and begins to accrue interest
March 1Second-half installment due, payable through March 31
AprilUnpaid second half becomes delinquent
By May 1Owner notice of the coming sale mailed first class (section 446.9)
One to three weeks before saleNotice published in an official county newspaper (section 446.9)
Third Monday in JuneAnnual tax sale

Late interest on delinquent installments is 1.5 percent per month, according to the Iowa treasurers' important dates page. A mortgagee or other interested party can ask for its own notice by filing a request one month before the sale with a $25 fee per parcel, valid five years.

sections.h2: Who can bid, and what does the winner get?
sections.html:
Bidders compete on percentage, and the lowest percentage wins. Bids must be at least one percent, and ties are settled by random selection (section 446.16). Bidders need a federal tax identification number and either a registered agent or a verified statement on file, and the treasurer may charge a reasonable registration fee.

If no one bids, or the bid falls below the total due, the county bids the total amount due, and no cash changes hands (section 446.19). Parcels left unsold for want of bidders can be offered again, and a county holding such a public bidder certificate may accept redemption any time before the deed issues.

The certificate holder pays later-year taxes and adds them to the amount the owner must redeem. The holder owns a claim to the parcel, not the parcel.

sections.h2: How much does it cost to redeem an Iowa tax sale parcel?
sections.html:
Redemption costs the sale amount, the certificate fee and later-year amounts, plus interest of 2 percent per month, with each fraction of a month counted as a full month (section 447.1). Interest has a $1 minimum, and payment must reach the treasurer by the last day of the month to avoid another month of interest.

  • Costs of serving the redemption notice, certified mail, any publication and the record search are added to the amount (section 447.13).
  • If the holder is not a county, the record search must be done by an Iowa title guaranty abstractor or an Iowa-licensed attorney, and the search charge is capped at $300.
  • Costs must be filed with the treasurer before redemption is complete, or the treasurer cannot collect them.

Since interest runs from the sale, a delay of even a few weeks can add another full month. A local treasurer can quote the exact payoff; for example, the Linn County Treasurer says its office processes redemptions and tells callers to phone 319-892-5500 for the fee and documents.

sections.h2: How long does an owner have before the right to redeem ends?
sections.html:
The right to redeem lasts at least until ninety days after the redemption notice is completely served. A certificate holder may serve that notice one year and nine months after the sale (section 447.9).

Type of saleEarliest redemption notice
Regular annual saleOne year and nine months after sale
Public bidder sale (446.18)Nine months after sale
Abandoned residential or vacant lot (446.19A) and public nuisance (446.19B) salesThree months after sale

The notice goes by regular and certified mail to the owner and the occupant, and to mortgagees and other record interest holders. If service cannot be made that way, the holder publishes it once in an official county newspaper. Service is complete only when an affidavit is filed with the treasurer, and the right of redemption then runs ninety days (section 447.12).

The deadline is close of business on day 90, or the next business day if day 90 is a weekend or holiday. A postmark does not count, so the payment itself must be received.

sections.h2: Are there protections for owners who cannot pay?
sections.html:
A few narrow ones exist. A county board of supervisors can redeem an owner-occupied residential parcel for an owner who is unable to contribute to public revenue, on petition (section 447.9(3)). A legal representative can redeem for a person with a legal disability before the deed is delivered, and after delivery that person has to bring an equitable action within one year after the disability is removed (section 447.7).

Notice also protects owners. If an owner of record was not served the redemption notice under section 447.9, the tax deed is void, subject to the affidavit rules in sections 448.15 and 448.16 (section 448.3).

These routes are limited. They do not replace paying the taxes or selling the home while the redemption right is still open.

sections.h2: What does an Iowa tax deed do?
sections.html:
The county treasurer issues the deed after the ninety-day period, and the deed vests the state's, the county's and the former owner's interest in the purchaser (sections 448.1 and 448.3). The treasurer records the deed before handing it over and receives $25 per deed.

A deed can be attacked only through an equitable action in district court, and the challenger must prove one of four things: the parcel was not subject to tax, the taxes were paid before the sale, the parcel was redeemed, or there was an entire omission in listing, assessment, levy, notice or sale (section 448.6). Such actions must be brought within three years after the deed is executed and recorded (section 448.12).

A deed holder in possession may also file an affidavit with the county recorder. Other claimants then have 120 days to file a claim and 60 more days to sue, and if no claim is filed, the title is conclusively established (sections 448.15 and 448.16).

Someone who remains in possession after a valid tax deed is subject to forcible entry and detainer (section 648.1).

sections.h2: Can I sell my Iowa house before the tax deed issues?
sections.html:
Yes, in most cases, because the owner keeps title until a deed is delivered. A sale that pays the redemption amount at closing ends the tax sale and clears that debt from the title.

Three practical steps help. Ask the county treasurer for a current redemption figure and the date interest next rolls over. Find out whether a redemption notice has been served, since that sets the ninety-day clock. And line up a buyer who can close before that clock runs out. Cash Home Buyers buys Iowa houses as-is and can move on a short timeline when the facts allow it, and we make no promise on price before reviewing the property.

faqs.q: When is the Iowa tax sale held?
faqs.a: The third Monday in June, unless the county treasurer sets a different June date for good cause.

faqs.q: What interest rate applies to Iowa tax sale redemption?
faqs.a: Two percent per month, and any fraction of a month counts as a full month. Costs and later-year taxes are added.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after the redemption notice?
faqs.a: Ninety days after service of the notice is complete. Payment must be received by close of business on day 90 or the next business day, and a postmark does not count.

faqs.q: Who issues an Iowa tax deed?
faqs.a: The county treasurer, after the ninety-day period, once the purchaser returns the certificate and pays the deed and recording fees.

faqs.q: Can a tax deed be challenged in Iowa?
faqs.a: Yes, but only in an equitable action in district court on narrow grounds, brought within three years of the deed being executed and recorded.

faqs.q: Does Iowa have a tax lien sale or a tax deed sale?
faqs.a: Iowa sells certificates of purchase at the annual sale, and a deed follows only if the property is not redeemed. The buyer's certificate works like a lien until then.
